speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TABLING OF P.C. 1513 VESTING RESPONSIBILITY IN MINISTER OF RECONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
The speech from the throne opening the present session of parliament forecast action to bring all matters relating to the construction of housing, as largely as possible under the administration of one minister of the crown. By order in council P.C. 1513 of April 16, 1946, the responsibility for housing has been vested in the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Hitherto, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has been responsible for the operations of Wartime Housing Limited, but other aspects of housing responsibility have been vested in the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Under the new arrangement, the responsibility for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which was established early this year under the Minister of Finance and which has responsibility for the administration of the National Housing Act and of the emergency shelter regulations, in addition to the financing of housing construction, will be transferred to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Arrangements have also been made to coordinate the operations carried on under the Veterans Land Act in relation to non-farm housing with the activities which will now centre in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply.
I wish to table a copy of order in council P.C. 1513 of April 16, in relation to housing.

subtopic: EDITORIAL IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"-REFERENCE TO EMPLOYMENT IN CIVIL SERVICE OF NATURALIZED CANADIANS

speechtext: On the order for motions:

subtopic: EDITORIAL IN "SATURDAY NIGHT"-REFERENCE TO EMPLOYMENT IN CIVIL SERVICE OF NATURALIZED CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. An editorial entitled "Classifying Canadians" appears in the current issue of Saturday Night. The first paragraph thereof reads as follows:
We should be sorry if parliament were to adopt Mr. Gordon Graydon's proposal and refuse to employ naturalised Canadians in the civil service. The further suggestion that even born Canadians be barred from the service if their parents were naturalized was. probably not intended very seriously.
The remainder of the editorial is devoted to a critical analysis of the position I am supposed to have taken. My purpose in rising is to say that at no time have I taken such a position or made such a proposal, and I fancy every hon. .member of the house will agree with me on that. I know that Saturday Night, whose columns are always characterized by fairness and reason, would want me to put the record straight at the first opportunity. This I am doing. Were the statement ito go unchallenged, a grave injustice unwittingly might easily be done to scores of thousands of loyal naturalized citizens of Canada, many of whom have served with high distinction in the last war and this. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I think it must have been a case of mistaken identity, but I have not been able to run it down yet. >

subtopic: RECOGNITION, OBSERVANCE AND COMMEMORATION- PROVISION FOR LEGAL HOLIDAY

speechtext: Mr. L. R. BEAUDOIN (Vaudreuil-Soulanges) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 58, respecting the recognition, observance and commemoration of Canadian citizenship.

subtopic: RECOGNITION, OBSERVANCE AND COMMEMORATION- PROVISION FOR LEGAL HOLIDAY
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: RECOGNITION, OBSERVANCE AND COMMEMORATION- PROVISION FOR LEGAL HOLIDAY
speechtext:
It is suggested by this bill, Mr. Speaker, that each year a day be set aside as citizenship day, a public occasion for the recognition of all who in consequence of the adoption of the Canadian citizenship act will have attained the status of Canadian citizens; a public occasion for all Canadians to develop mutual understanding and promote national unity.
I know the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) will endeavour to provide effective and impressive ceremonies for the admission of new

Canadian Citizenship

Canadians into the Canadian family. The house agreed with him when he said, as reported at page 504 of Hansard:
One thing wTe hope to do, following the passage of this measure-
That is, the Canadian citizenship bill.
-is to provide a more effective and impressive ceremony for admission ipto the Canadian family.
Also when he said:
We are convinced of the desirability of emulating the form of ceremony which characterizes the admisssion of persons into United States citizenship.	,
Canada may want to emulate the form of celebration, which does not interfere with admission ceremonies, instituted by the United States on May 3, 1940, which takes place on the third Sunday in May of each year, and is designated as "I am an American" day. This bill proposes to create "I am a Canadian" day. Service clubs, social organizations and other institutions in Canada have shown their willingness to do the spade-work to bring this sort of celebration into being. For instance, at one of their annual conventions the junior chambers of commerce of Canada adopted a resolution in which they suggested a special citizenship week each year, which would be called Canada week, and I am informed that such a move is now being organized, with the period fixed as June 2 to June 8 next. Let us give these patriotic organizations our encouragement; and a debate on this bill, should it take place, I am sure will bring out most valuable suggestions. Incidentally I would hope that the proclamation of our official flag might coincide with the proclamation of our citizenship bill.
The purpose of this bill is to help Canadians, old and new, especially the older Canadians who are supposed to set the good examples and lead the way for the new, not only to realize and take pride in the achievements and the greatness of Canada but to promote national unity by reminding all of us of our present status and future aspirations as a nation. According to this bill, each year throughout Canada the anniversary of the day fixed by proclamation of the governor in council as the date of coming into force of the Canadian citizenship act, which it has been said "symbolizes our aspirations as a nation" shall be a legal holiday, kept and observed as such under the name of "Canadian citizenship day".
Let me close my explanations with these words of the Secretary of State when intro-

ducing the Canadian citizenship bill on October 1, 1945, and again on the motion for second reading of the bill on April 2, 1946:
For the national unity of Canada and for the future and greatness of this country it is felt to be of the utmost importance that all of us, new Canadians or old, have a consciousness of a common purpose and common interests as Canadians; that all of us be able to say with pride and say with meaning-
And may I add, to proclaim at least once a year, in some sort of official and solemn way: "I am a Canadian citizen."
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: MOUNTED POLICE-RANK AND SENIORITY UPON RETURN FROM OVERSEAS SERVICE
speechtext:
1.	At the outbreak of war the Minister of Justice made an appeal by letter to all ranks of the R.C.M. Police to stay at their, posts, owing to the increased responsibilities of the force, and the impossibility of securing recruits, and in order to make it more difficult to leave the force, the normal means of discharge by purchase, etc., were suspended.
In order to assist the military authorities, and at the same time provide a channel for those members of the force who were anxious to join the fighting forces, No. 1 Provost Company of the First Canadian Division was organized within the force in October, 1939, and the police personnel which composed that company, together with reinforcements, were granted leave of absence without pay. All these retained rank, seniority and other privileges.
Furthermore, those who later severed their connection with the R.C.M. Police at the time of the expiration of their engagement with the R.C.M. Police and joined the armed forces of Canada and served overseas, on reengagement in the R.C.M. Police have been reinstated in their former rank, pay, allowances and seniority, with the exception of N.C.O.'s who lose seniority only. (Seven N.C.O.'s are thus affected, having left the Force to accept commissions in the armed services).

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, April 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin for the second reading of bill No. 7, respecting citizenship, nationality, naturalization and status of aliens.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I moved the adjournment of the debate, and I am ready to continue. During the Easter recess I felt that I could not do better than to make the widest possible investigation as to the opinion of the average man in the great counties of Grey, Wellington, Perth, Middlesex, Kent, Essex and parts of Elgin and Peel, as well as in my own riding in Toronto and other ridings in that city, about Bill No. 7, particularly section 10.
Generally I am in agreement with the bill. I believe there are a number of sections that should pass, but/I am opposed to part of section 10. I spent some time in the riding of the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) who introduced this bill. In that part of the country, and in the other parts to which I referred, I spoke to as many people as I could, high and low and in all walks of life, and I found a substantial opposition to section 10. Many of these people said that the section was incomprehensible to them. Some had come to this country from other parts of the empire, particularly from Great Britain; they had come from a part of the world in which they had learned democracy and from which they had brought the spirit of democracy to this country. They represent by far the largest majority of Canadians, and to me it is simply monstrous to ask that they have to be here five years before they can be granted Canadian- citizenship.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: It has been that way for twenty-seven years.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: My hon. friend is entirely wrong. He knows that a man coming into this country from Great Britain to-day is permitted after one year to enrol and vote in our general elections whether he is a citizen or not.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: This bill does not disturb that at all.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
Anything might happen after section 10 has carried. The next step will be to change the franchise act so that
.
only citizens may vote. I am going to appeal to the minister to state when he speaks again that section 10 will be rewritten. As it is now, only a Philadelphia lawyer could understand it. Britishers should not be compelled to remain here five years before being granted Canadian citizenship. My own people have been here for four generations. Had they come only one generation ago, it would have been monstrous to ask them to remain here five years before being granted the right to citizenship. I spoke to clergymen of various denominations, to lawyers, to doctors, to business men, to garage men, to barbers, and to everyone whom I could engage in conversation. If, as the minister says, section 10 does not mean what I think it means, then it should be clarified.
I have discussed this section with several lawyers, both in and out of the house, and they tell me that they cannot understand what it really means. I suppose even a Philadelphia lawyer could not understand it. To indicate the opinion of the public with regard to section 10, I should like to quote one letter I have received. If this bill passes and persons from the British empir-e are forced to remain here five years before being granted Canadian citizenship, then, as I said a moment ago, the next step will be to change the franchise act to provide that only citizens may vote.
That was one cause of the South African war. The then president of the Transvaal, the late Paul Kruger, who in my judgment was a wonderful man; I have read 'his history many times-decided to amend the franchise act of the Transvaal to provide for several years' residence instead of what it then provided before obtaining the right to vote. That will be. the next step -here, and Anglo-Saxons may have to remain here five years before they have the right to vote. It is incredible that any such provision should be made part of our law. When the minister speaks I should like him to clarify this section-apparently very few people can understand it; then perhaps the bill will get through the house more rapidly.
I received a letter this morning from St. George's society in Toronto quoting a telegram which they had sent to the Prime Minister. It is dated at Toronto, April 16, 1946, and the telegram quoted therein reads as follows:
Twelve hundred members of St. George's society of Toronto, while heartily approving the principle of establishing a Canadian citizenship, nevertheless deplore that provision of the proposed act of parliament requiring British subjects to be domiciled for five years in Can-

Canadian Citizenship
ada prior to enjoying the privilege of such citizenship. Such a measure cannot fail to weaken the ties of empire at a time when they need strengthening.
This opinion therefore is general, because, as my hon. friend will freely admit, many leading citizens of Toronto and Canada are members of the St. George's society.
When the minister spoke on April 2 he quoted in support of his own argument a statement which had been -made in the house by the late Hon. C.. H. Cahan. I was present when Mr. Cahan spoke. He was an excellent speaker, and perhaps one of the greatest constitutional lawyers in Canada. He was referring to the progress made by Canada in the sixty-four years of its life from 1867, and he went on to say, as quoted by the minister:
In connection with that development, however, if we are to assume the status of a nation within the British commonwealth, we must also assume very serious duties and responsibilities. Among the responsibilities resting upon the parliament of Canada is that of framing a clear definition of "Canadian nationals" . . .
With that I agree, but I want especially to emphasize what the late Hon. C. H. Cahan said, "within the British commonwealth". Section 10, as I understand it, will do a lot more harm to the cause of maintaining Canada within the British empire than perhaps many of us want to believe.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: It will not change it one iota.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: Of course the minister has the majority behind him and has power to do what he likes, but that will not stop me from expressing my opinion.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext: I was not suggesting that. I was simply saying that section 10 does not change what the hon. member wants, and what I personally support. It does not change that situation at all.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OP ALIENS
speechtext:
I have found from inquiries across eight or ten great counties of Ontario that many people have the same opinion that I have of section 10, and I repeat that St. George's Society, one of the leading societies of Canada, is of that opinion. We are all in the same boat; we do not understand it, so if the minister can clarify the section and can take away our fears it would go a long way towards eliminating opposition to this particular provision of the bill.
My own section of the city of Toronto is solidly Anglo-Saxon. The great majority of the people came there two or three years before the first great war. They took an ardent and active interest in the affairs of this country. They formed their own rifle associations and other groups, and when the war of 1914
broke out they did not have to be conscripted or coaxed to come to the defence of their country; they marched right up, like the men they were, and enlisted en masse. The society of which I was president, the British Imperial Association, had a great honour roll. Speaking from memory I think there were from 200 to 300 men on its honour roll who went overseas, and a great many of whom were killed in the defence of this country. I could not conceive of that breed of people coming to Canada if they thought they would have to remain five years within a part of the British empire before they could become citizens of Canada.
A gentleman told me to-day-I think it was the member for London (Mr. Manross)- about an Australian airman who had trained at an air camp in western Ontario-I had better not specify it because I did not have the hon. member's consent to say what I am about to say. This Australian airman had the good fortune to fall in love with a London girl, and perhaps has married her, but on reading over this bill he said that Australians could not be expected to come to Canada and remain here for five years before they could become Canadian citizens. Nor can we expect New Zealanders or South Africans or people from any other part of the British empire to come here if they have to wait five years before they can become Canadian citizens- unless they want very much to come here; and the more they want to come, the more we want to have them come. We do not want to discourage people from coming to Canada from other parts of the British empire. We should do everything we can to encourage them to come, because the greater the number that come the better it is for Canada and the British empire, as was demonstrated clearly in the last war. From my own section of the city of Toronto the sons of the fathers who came back to Canada from the first great war enlisted en masse in the second great war. They did not have to be conscripted or coaxed. They marched up and enlisted in regiments very shortly after the war broke out. That is the kind of people we want to come here, men who will rise up in defence of this country and the ideals for which it stands. We should not do anything to discourage them from coming to Canada.
A few days ago I read that the Ontario government has a list of selected emigrants from Great Britain, some 30,000 people, most of them war veterans, who want to come to Canada as soon as immigration opens up again. Canadian Citizenship
Paul was a citizen of the city of Tarsus and of the Roman province of Cilicia. He did not go back on his Roman citizenship. He was a citizen of the Roman empire. We are Canadians. Before long, I suppose, we shall be citizens of Canada legally, but it does not take away from us our right to be British citizens. We shall be British citizens as well as Canadian citizens.
I feel very strongly on this matter. The minister has not convinced me at all. I find myself in the same position as the members of St. George's Society, and of many other societies from whom I have had communications. I find myself in the same position as are the people to whom I talked during the Easter holidays. If I said I talked to a hundred people I should be understating it. If I said I talked to 250 during my tour of western Ontario last week I might be overstating it. However, I could not find one man among the lawyers, doctors, business men and educationists to whom I spoke, whose interpretation of the bill was any different from mine. Therefore a lot of clarification has to be done to make people realize that Britishers coming into Canada from any part of the empire are not compelled to remain here five years before they become Canadian citizens.
I have read the section over carefully; I have discussed it with all the lawyers on this side of the house. My hon. friend will have to admit that they are good lawyers; if I happened to get into a bad jam I do not know which one I would want to select to defend me. All of them interpret this section as I do, namely, that anyone coming into this country from any other part of the British empire would have to remain here five years before he would be entitled to become a Canadian citizen. To that I am opposed. It is a humiliation to ask a New Zealander, an Australian, a Scotsman, an Irishman, an Englishman, a Newfoundlander, or anyone from any other part of the British empire to remain here five years before Canadian citizenship papers can be taken- out.

Generally, Mr. Speaker, I support the bill, but I should like to speak to one or two points in connection with it. First I should like to say a word or two in regard to the revocation of citizenship. I believe citizenship should not be lightly granted, but that once granted it should be practically irrevocable. This measure provides for the cancellation of Canadian citizenship in certain circumstances, including the commission of certain types of crimes. The last time this matter was under discussion the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) made a great point, of the fact a person of Japanese origin, and I think a Canadian citizen, had tortured some of our Canadian soldiers at Hong Kong. If Canadians commit crimes, let them be punished as Canadians. Let them be put in gaol as Canadians. If necessary let us shoot them as Canadians, but let us deal with them as Canadians. Let us accept responsibility for their upbringing and their environment.
Some would avoid such responsibility by a method of which as yet we have not had an example in this country; that is to say, by deportation. The other day I put a question on the order paper and was told that not a

Canadian Citizenship

single person of Japanese origin, Canadian citizen or otherwise, as yet had been deported from this country. But deportation is a dangerous policy. The force of circumstances and international conflicts make our friends of to-day our enemies to-morrow. I need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the Japanese, who were our deadly enemies in the war which has just come to a conclusion, were our firm friends and allies in the last war. If you make of citizenship a scrap of paper to be tom up at will, to be tom up in the panic and hatreds of war; if you deport people of one racial origin to-day, to-morrow you may be deporting people of another racial origin. What about the many fine Canadian citizens of German origin? Would this government propose to deport them? And who are our native Canadians, anyway, unless they be the Indians?-and we are not too sure about them. Let us think twice, then, before breaking our solemn word to people whom we have accepted as citizens of this country.
The second point I should like to make is that we should not be apologetic about being Canadians. In my opinion in the past we have suffered from a distinct inferiority complex. To-day in this country there are people, and even whole sections, still suffering from the same inferiority complex. It has plagued us in our arts and in our literature, and I think it extends even to our citizenship. Let us be proud of our own country. As the hon. member for Temis-couata, Mr. Pouliot is so fond of reminding us, this is the greatest country in the world. WHat, then, is the citizenship of which we should be so proud?. Well, as far as I am concerned it has nothing whatever to do with racial origin. I have been astonished to hear hon. members of this house boasting about the place of their birth. Could they tell us just what they had to do with it? if you were born in Canada it is a matter not for boasting but for thankfulness, particularly when we look at other countries and see how they and their people have been decimated by the flames of war. No; as I see it, citizenship should not be judged on the basis of racial origin. It is not just a racial ribbon to be worn on your coat. It means the contribution which one makes to the environment in which he finds himself. To me that is citizenship. It is the custom of my Tory friends to my right to protest their loyalty, but methinks they do protest too much.

My understanding is that the bill asks for nothing new. If through its operation one were to lose the right to vote, it would be in an entirely different category, and I would discuss it from a different point of view. I agree with the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) that subsequently the franchise and election acts may have to be changed to conform with the bill. That is within the realm of possibility, and when it so decides it is the right of parliament to make that change. We should discuss the matter in the light of circumstances which then exist. But if any such action is ever taken I should like to see a distinction made between those who come to Canada from a country in which the institutions and language are different from ours, and those who come from countries-and I use the plural-in which there are democratic institutions analogous to our own, whether the United States, the United Kingdom, or one of the commonwealth nations.

The hon. member for Davenport went to great lengths in discussing the desirability of bringing in 30,000 British people who have applied to come to this country. I should like to see them come, but I would remind the hon. member that the government he supported between 1930 and 1935 deported over 30,000 British citizens whose only crime against this country was that they could not find jobs and were on relief. I know that to be true; the records and statistics will bear out my statement. As a member of the city council of Regina at that time I know that when we applied to the federal authorities for certain assistance we were told that some of these people had to be deported because they were public charges. As public charges they were deportable within the five years that Sir Robert Borden laid down as the length of domicile which a British citizen must have in this country before he could not be deported. Let us not forget that when we hear this bill attacked on the ground that it is doing something entirely new which is endangering the rights of British citizens in this country. As a Canadian citizen in the right of the King of Canada, that is a Canadian subject. He would be separate and distinct because the sovereign is separate and distinct. To my mind that is the way to view this. It would not for one moment affect our allegiance to a common sovereign, but it would make our citizenship what it ought to be, something distinct, something in which we can have pride as citizens of Canada.
I should like to go one step further. Anyone who comes to Canada should receive some certificate of citizenship. The length of residence need not be the same. It could be five years for those who are not used to our institutions; it could be one, two or three years for those who come from countries in which there are democratic institutions and language similar to our own. We cannot dodge the fact that there are two types of people who come to this country from other parts of the British commonwealth. There is the type of person who comes here to make Canada his home, who comes here to become a part of the great citizenship and family of Canada. This is the man who establishes his family in this country and intends to be in every respect a citizen of the country as long as he shall live. There are others who come here and stay one, two, five, ten or fifteen years but never regard this country as their homeland, and always look forward to the time when they can return home. Such a citizen has not the same loyalty to Canada as the one who makes this country his permanent home.

I hear my hon. friend say, "the Chinaman." It is true that some Chinese have that conception, but some people who were bom in the country in which I was born also have the same conception. They came to this country never expecting to stay. I know many of them who have always regarded the little isles across the sea as the place to which they are going to return, their homeland. I think we should teach all our people that if this country is good enough to make a living in, if it is good enough to establish a home in, then their loyalty should be to the country in which they live. That would not take one thing away from the broader loyalty which we feel as citizens of that great family which we call the British commonwealth, independent citizens equal with one another, owing allegiance to the same king, with the same symbol of unity. To my mind that is the dignified position in which any Canadian, Australian, New Zealander or Britisher should find himself. Those of us who have been here for many years, who have established our homes in this country, would not receive anything to show that' we are citizens of this country. Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to make any lengthy observations with respect to the measure which is now before the house for second reading. But I wish to make as earnest, as strong and as emphatic a plea as I can for the adoption of what I believe to be the proper procedure with respect to this bill. In discussing matters such as citizenship quite often the people of this nation are subconsciously divided when there is really no real reason for division. I have always felt
Canadian Citizenship

I was fortunate in being able to approach subjects of this kind without very much heat, although on many occasions subjects have been brought forward in this connection where heat seems to have been very easily generated.
It always interests me to hear people talk as if they were better Canadians than other people, but I have never found it easy to find a dividing line and say that on this side the people are all good Canadians and on that side bad Canadians. Human nature is not built that way. There are very few people in this house of Commons who have a greater affection for the old British Isles than I have and I do not think anyone need ask me to apologize for that position, which I have taken a good many times. On the other hand I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the house that I do not think that that affection should be regarded by anybody in the house as making us any less a Canadian than anybody else in Canada. I like to think that it makes us as good Canadians in any event as anybody else. I am not one of those who believe that any class or section of our people have a monopoly on good Canadianism in this country. You find good Canadianism in all sections of Canada, and I hope that we shall find that condition to continue to exist through all the years.
I have often felt that we might perhaps take a leaf out of the book of the British people themselves in developing a love of country. One of the things which struck me when I was overseas for the first time last November, December and January was the great love of country that I saw displayed everywhere I went in the British Isles, and I liked that feeling. In these days when we are spreading ourselves very thin in the international field, some may regard it as not being in the interests of world unity to express our affection too loudly for our own people and our own country, but I am not so sure that that kind of doctrine holds water. I think that the best contribution which this country can make to the commonwealth, to the empire and to the world organization is to develop a united Canada, a great country of our own, and at the same time develop a great love and affection for this land of ours.
I noticed everywhere I went in Britain that the people had a great and consuming affection for that land and I would like to see in this country no less a consuming affection for our own country and for our own people than the British have for theirs. Because, Mr. Speaker, this is a great land, great not

only in its own right, but a great land to which the nations of the world are turning their eyes to-day as a country where people can live and find employment in the years that lie ahead. There is not a country in Europe where there are not thousands and scores of thousands of people who desire to emigrate to Canada. Why? Because this is regarded as one of the great lands of opportunity in the future world. If that is the view of other nations, surely it can be the view of a united Canadian people as well.
There comes to my mind at the moment an example of the type of affection I saw exhibited by the people of the old land for their own people and their own country. It was when we were leaving Southampton on one of the Clyde-built Queens, the Mary. There were on board at that time some 1,700 British war brides, with some 600 children, coming to rejoin on this side of the water American husbands whom they had married overseas. The scene left an indelible impression on my mind. As we left the dock at Southampton these girls lined the rails of the ship to take their last look at Britain and I have never seen as great a demonstration of affection not just for their families, their relatives and those who were close to them, but for their native land which they were leaving and which meant so much to them. I think in this country we do not do quite enough of that. We need to develop in Canada-I think we are all guilty in this respect, in most cases thoughtlessly guilty- the same kind of national pride, if you like, and I do not apologize for using that word, and the same kind of national affection for our country and for our people that has made the United Kingdom so great. You can perhaps rebuild devastated political structures; you can perhaps rebuild devastated economic structures, and these things are all-important in their place, but what is of the greatest national importance are the spiritual values in the nation itself. Those spiritual values comprise many things. One of the component parts of the spiritual values in this nation as in any other nation is the faith and confidence we have in ourselves as a nation and that love of country which has been so effective in building and maintaining and preserving other great nations of the world.
I make this appeal to the House of Commons this afternoon with great sincerity and with every emphasis at my command. I would like to see in the years that lie ahead the development in this country of a pride and an affection among ourselves for our own people and for our own country. I think in

Canadian Citizenship
the end that would mean a great deal and be the greatest contribution to the success of this nation and to its prestige in the empire and among the other nations of the world.
Before closing my rambling and very impromptu remarks this afternoon I would suggest to the minister that he give consideration now to the procedure to be followed in considering this bill. I regard this bill as a very important piece of legislation, so important that we cannot afford to toy with it. It is so important, that we cannot afford to give it anything less than our very best attention and the most careful consideration of which this house and parliament is capable. All through the years it has been the experience of most of us who have been in parliament for any length of time that with a very important measure such as this, with many sections and great detail, the procedure that has been found most successful and effective in bringing forward the best type of legislation is to refer the bill after second reading, where the importance of the measure warrants it, to a committee of the House of Commons. You ask why? I could give many reasons, but in this particular instance there are two that are of exceptional importance. If, as I understand, it is the government's intention, unless they change it, to bring the bill before the committee of the whole, there will be no opportunity to do more than examine the minister with reference to its various provisions. He will be before the committee of the whole, assisted, and ably assisted, by his deputy, and our questions will, of course, be answered from time to time. But that is not enough on a bill such as this. This bill requires the best that this house can give it, and the committee of the whole is not, in my opinion, the best machinery available to members for the consideration of the measure. We should have the benefit of the crossexamination, if you like, or at any rate the questioning of the members of his department and those particular officials who have been working on the bill, to see after careful review by a committee, such as that on external affairs whether we can come to a conclusion which in the years to come will render it unnecessary for other governments, for this government or for any other parliament in some other session, to amend the bill in any respect. I should like to see a good job done on the bill now, and I am not satisfied that the best job can be done under the procedure to which the minister now seems so wedded.
I would suggest as my second reason, and the minister must' of course be aware of this, that many points of view with respect to a
matter such as this ought, in my opinion to be aired, if that is the desire, then the members of any committee that might deal with the bill ought to be given an opportunity to consider those views, so that no stone would be left unturned in seeing that this is the best measure that can be brought forward on such a vital and important national subject as citizenship and nationality.
I am going to make an appeal to the minister. I know there are reasons against this course which to him may appear valid and cogent. But we, too, have some views as well, and views that are strongly held, which dictate the course that we now propose. I am going to ask the minister to reconsider the matter, to review the whole question of the government's policy with respect to the procedure now being adopted. If the minister will reflect carefully, if the government will look into' the matter from this point of view, they will see that by putting the bill before the committee of the whole instead of submitting it to a special committee they are doing less than justice to a bill to which, I submit, we cannot afford to do less than full justice, having in mind the special position it occupies in the legislation before this parliament.

The first Canadians, if we may call them such, were the Indians who resided in this country when the first white men came. When we try to go back to the time of the arrival in Canada of the first white men I think we in the maritimes can claim that the first white Canadians settled there. In recalling our history we shall remember that the first white settlement was founded at Port Royal in Nova Scotia, the city of Quebec being founded, I believe, four or five years afterwards.

We in New Brunswick are called herring-chokers and over in Prince Edward Island they are known as spud-islanders or some such appellation as that. speechtext:
In concluding this debate
it was not my intention to make any protracted statement, and perhaps in some respects it may not be necessary in the light of the fact that the measure has received such wide approval in principle from all sections of the house; but because during the course of the debate attention has been paid to two points in the bill, and because on account of the rules of the house there was no opportunity to make a full statement with regard to some of the points made by hon. gentlemen opposite, it does seem desirable to take advantage of this opportunity to correct certain misapprehensions which have been expressed during the, course of the debate.
As the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said to-day, the measure before the house is an important one. It was carefully studied by a committee of the departments of External Affairs, Justice, Immigration and the Department qf the Secretary of State. I wish to pay tribute to-night to a number of men from these departments who were associated with me over many weeks in the preparation of this important measure. We had the advantage of having before us not only our own proposals but also the studies made by a former secretary of state to whom I made reference in this debate when I moved second reading.
First of all, I should like to express my gratification at the degree of unanimity and approval that has been shown in the speeches which have been made. I think it would not be too much to say that almost every hon. member has approved the principle embodied in the bill. This is of particular importance in a measure of this kind; for it might be called an organic measure, a measure that will go into and become part of the basic legal framework of Canada. The highest possible degree of general approval is always of greatest importance for such a fundamental piece of legislation.
In addition, however, there is the fact that this bill is intended to aid in creating a sense of unity and oneness in Canada, a feeling of community. A bill to create unity must not be based on disunity and disagreement. It is therefore particularly pleasing -to see the measure of support which the bill has been receiving.
I do not wish to discuss the general aspects of the bill at any length at this time, but there are two parts of it which have caused some discussion and to which I would wish to make reference. The portions I have in mind
are embodied in sections 10 and 26 of the bill. The parts of section 10 that have received particular attention are the requirements which are imposed by way of qualification and procedure on non-Canadian British subjects who desire to become Canadian citizens. The question in relation to section 26 is whether the bill should provide that the status of British subject continues for Canadian citizens. In my opening statement I said that this bill parallels the development of Canada as a nation. I repeat that statement.
This bill cannot and does not seek to meet extreme points of view which in some instances have been expressed in this house. There are extreme positions that can be taken in connection with these points. At one end of the scale there is the desire to reduce the qualification and procedure for non-Canadian British subjects to the minimum and to emphasize as much as possible the status of British subjects for Canadian citizens. At the other end of the scale the position is that no privileges whatever should be given to British subjects; that they should be aliens in the sight of our law and that the status of British subject should be eliminated with regard to Canadian citizens. These are extreme points of view. The present bill does not go to either extreme. For that reason it does not secure complete approval from either of the groups of opinion to which I have referred. The bill falls in between that. It assumes a middle position, and I think a reasonable position, one that enjoys, I believe, a greater measure of general support among the Canadian people than either of the more extreme positions would elicit.
First of all let me refer to the position of the non-Canadian British subjects. Particular criticism has been directed against the requirement of five years' residence, and against the procedure involved in the acquisition of a certificate. Before examining these matters, let me. state categorically what I have said before by way of interjection and by way of my statement at the opening of the debate, but what has so frequently been ignored or forgotten, that the bill will not and does not remove one iota of the rights and privileges that are now enjoyed by British subjects in Canada. A British subject over twenty-one has now the right to vote. He will continue to have that right to vote after this bill is passed. A British subject is eligible for an old age pension. He will continue to be eligible for an old age pension after the bill is passed. A British subject is eligible for appointment to the civil service. He will continue to be eligible for such appointment after the bill is passed.
Canadian Citizenship

The rights that British subjects now have will remain in full. None is taken away by this bill or reduced in any respect. They remain precisely as they are. The bill does not affect the status of British subjects in any way; it merely regulates the method of becoming Canadian citizens.
Moreover, under the bill-and no attention has been paid to this fact-all those British subjects now in Canada who have domicile will become citizens of Canada on the passage of this bill. The wives of soldiers, the war brides who are coming and who will be coming to Canada in the next few months, will automatically become Canadian citizens under this bill. These two facts have not been emphasized.
The suggestion has been made from one extreme quarter that this bill was an attempt to violate Canada's relationship to the commonwealth. No reference was made by these, hon. gentlemen to the provision of section 26 of the bill winch in its precise terms are more definite than will be found in any corresponding legislation in any other part of the commonwealth. On the other hand, those who took exception to the fact that the bill provides that Canadian citizens shall be designated British subjects failed to recogize that the paramount status in the bill is the status of being able to say, "I am a Canadian citizen."
No one can envisage the future. In 1919, when Sir Robert Borden changed the provision from three years to five years, he was faced within his own party by the very sort of argument which has been used by some hon. gentlemen during this debate. The rights- of British subjects were not changed by the amendments brought in by the government of Sir Robert Borden, any more than they will be changed to-day. This parliament, representing as it does the temper, the opinion and the conviction of the Canadian people, will always be guided by the character of Canada, a free nation within the British commonwealth. In some references which have been made to the bill, it has been suggested that the five-year requirement is something new, which never existed 'before. In actual fact it is nothing of the sort. The requirement of five years' residence as it applies to British subjects is exactly the same to-day as it has been since 1919. Thus it is simply a continuation of the existing provision.
In essence, citizenship is made up of a collection of rights and duties that pertain to a particular status. Some of the rights are internal to the state involved, and some are external. The former group are fairly clear: the right to own property, the right to vote,

the right of appointment to. particular positions, the right to pension and so forth. The external rights are also fairly clear. Normally they include the right to be admitted into the country on coming to its boundaries, the right to diplomatic and consular protection and assistance, the right to a passport and so forth. As far as Canada is concerned, the internal rights, if I may call them such, are accorded to British subjects on the same basis as to Canadian citizens. As I have already emphasized, none of this will be changed with the passage of this bill. As far as the external rights are concerned, the one normally most important is the right of entry, and for almost half a century this right has been limited to Canadian citizens and other persons having their domicile here. The British subject who comes to the shores of Canada has no right of entry. If he is admitted to Canada as an immigrant and lives here for five years he becomes a Canadian citizen under the Immigration Act, and only then does he have an automatic right to come into Canada.
When this requirement of a number of years of residence was first imposed the period was two years. That was prior to 1910. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was perhaps the only hon. member who very properly pointed out that this period was required for certain reasons, mainly health and to avoid the mischief of individuals whose records were clearly those of criminals. The period was required in order to give the immigration authorities a chance to see whether the person was desirable to have as a Canadian; whether he was sound in body and mind; whether he had criminal tendencies, and so on. Later, the two-year period was found to 'be too short, and in 1910, at the request of the provinces it was extended to three years. However, as I said earlier, this also was found to be inadequate and in 1919 a Conservative government under the leadership of Sir Robert Borden extended the period from three to five years, where it has remained ever since. In short, for over a quarter of a century we have required five years' residence of a British subject before granting him a right of entry.
Perhaps one more word might be said on this point. Obviously a bill such as that now before the house must be related to the Immigration Act. When we come to deal with this particular section my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), speaking as Minister of Immigration, will relate to the house some of the difficulties being experienced by his department, and will show statistically how important this provision really is. I may say frankly that

Canadian Citizenship
when the bill was being discussed we had taken the position that it might be desirable to reduce the period, but that met with objections on the part of the officers of the department of immigration. They are by no means, by their own traditions, men who can be said to be inimical to the interests of the British commonwealth. Every hon. member knows from what part of the world came the commissioner of immigration, who has to administer this measure. Everyone, of course, knows the origin of the Minister of Mines and Resources, if there should be any doubt about my own sincerity in the matter. But from the point of view of administration, having in mind the desirability that we should not be saddled with people who had criminal records, people who were of criminal tendencies or people who had mental difficulties not ascertained or ascertainable at the time of entry; having in mind that provincial institutions were being called upon to take care of many of these people, it was felt desirable that we should not be saddled within one or two or three years with the burden of maintaining them, when for the greater part of their lives they had resided elsewhere.
I think the relevance of what I have said will be apparent, for it completes the picture with regard to British subjects and makes it clear that their rights have not been changed in the present bill. The rights that British subjects have enjoyed, as British subjects, will continue to be theirs; they do not have to be Canadian citizens in order to secure them. On the other hand, the right of entry, which hitherto they have been able to obtain after five years of residence, will continue.to be theirs after five years of residence. The time element is nothing new; it is no change whatsoever. It does not alter the position of a British subject; it merely perpetuates a situation which has prevailed in this countiy for over a quarter of a century.
During the debate the question was asked: "Why should it be necessary to give a certificate of citizenship to a non-Canadian British subject?" Well, I could understand that attitude on the part of someone who perhaps has had no experience in the administration of the immigration department, or the administration of the Department of the Secretary of State, or the administration of the Department of External Affairs, or to a lesser extent, the administration of the Department of Justice. But let me give the house one case that came to my attention only after six o'clock this afternoon. A few days ago the daughter of a well known missionary of the United Church, who had been in China for
over twenty-three years, proceeded to the United States to attend university. She had never lived in this country. Her father had been born in the United Kingdom and had come to Canada, where he was ordained in the United church ministry and almost immediately thereafter went to China. Under the laws of China that girl is a citizen of that country. She is not a citizen of the United Kingdom, but she is a citizen of Canada. She was on her way to a particular university in the United States, but in the middle of the night an immigration officer instructed her to get up and prepare to answer certain questions. Later, she was put off the train because she could not prove to that officer that she was a citizen of Canada. She had nothing by way of documentary proof to show that she was not, even in her own mind, a citizen of China. Will anyone say that under those circumstances we should perpetuate that kind of injustice? As my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources will show later on, the immigration department is full of cases of that sort, clearly indicating that in the interests of justice itself to thousands of individuals it is wholly desirable that they should have documentary proof of the citizenship which the existing law or which this measure will give them.

The second general matter with which I wish to deal is the provision in the bill for the maintenance of the status of British subject. From the remarks of certain hon. members it is apparent that there is a large measure of misunderstanding as to the reason for having the sections which deal with the status of British subject. I think it has been generally felt that the principle involved in sections 26 and 28 is of such importance that the bill cannot be properly dealt with on second reading without referring to them in some detail.
Section 26 states that a Canadian citizen is a British subject. What does this mean? Does it mean that a Canadian citizen is a subject of Great Britain? It most certainly does not. No one needs to tell hon. members of the Canadian parliament that the independence of Canada is complete. Canadians are subject to the authority of no government outside Canada. No matter what they may be called, they are as Canadians subject to no other country. There is no possible room for doubt on this point.
Does the section means that we are demanding special favours for Canadians? Are we calling them British subjects in order to require of other countries of the commonwealth that they be given special treatment? Some hon. members have suggested that that is so. In reality, it is not so. The government of the United Kingdom is not obliged to give any special treatment to all persons who happen to bear the generic name "British subject". It can differentiate among them as much as it wishes, and give as many or as few rights and privileges as it sees fit. The government of Australia can treat Australian-British subjects in one way and Canadian-British subjects in another. It can differentiate between Cana-
 '
dlan-British subjects and South African-British subjects. It can do precisely as it wishes, no matter what term of description we may use. The same is true for all other governments of the commonwealth. Each one is completely free to give or deny rights to British subjects as a whole or to any part of that broad group. Such differentiation and distinction has been a fact for years, and it will continue to be a fact.

As a result, it is clear that when we say "A Canadian citizen is a British subject", we ask no recognition from anyone for any particular implications as flowing from the title. Whatever rights or privileges another country gives to Canadian citizens will depend on their law-not on ours.. Nothing we may do can. in any way limit their full and free capacity to treat our citizens on whatever basis they see fit in so far as their law is concerned.
There is a third possibility as to the meaning of the section. Is it necessary to ensure that a Canadian citizen is a subject of His Majesty the King? Again the answer is no. It is, of course, beyond doubt that a Canadian citizen is and will be a subject of the king, but that does not depend in any way upon the force of this section. There is no magic in the appellation "British subject", and a Canadian citizen would as surely and as loyally ow,e allegiance to the crown whether we called him "British subject" or not. Loyalty does not depend on a name, and it would be a rash man who would suggest that a Canadian would be less loyal as a "Canadian citizen" than he would be as a "British subject". The

Canadian Citizenship
fact of allegiance exists. The spirit of loyalty is beyond doubt. Section 26 could go without affecting our loyalty or the fact of our allegiance in any way.
Those, then, are three possibilities that do not apply. Section 26 does not mean subjection to Great Britain. It does not constitute a demand for special treatment. It is not essential to maintain our loyalty to the crown.
What then does section 26 mean when it says that "a Canadian citizen is a British subject?" It means nothing more or less than that we are retaining a term which has been used traditionally to designate a particular group of people in the world who share a peculiar association, of which association we have been and are a part. There is a definite practical reason for retaining the term, but before coming to that I wish to deal with some more general considerations.
Some people have questioned whether the retention of this term does not conflict with one purpose of the bill, which is to foster a sense of Canadianism. I do not think that it does or that it hinders us in any way. Because the name "British subject" implies no inflexible rights and duties we are able to retain it and still be completely free to legislate as we wish. It does not impose anything on us or deny anything from us. Moreover, there is, I think, a positive value in retaining this symbol of our association in the British commonwealth of nations. The commonwealth has been and is a great force for good in the world, and there is much to be said for preserving some of the evidences of association that do not conflict or interfere in any way with the essentials of our separate personality and status. The government is of the opinion that this house and the people of Canada will, on the whole, agree that the term should be retained.

Yes. From the practical point of view, however, there is an important reason for retaining the term "British subject". While it is not a term that has any specific meaning in terms of rights and duties, it has acquired the character of a technical legal term that has become so firmly embedded in our law, particularly our statute law, both provincial and dominion, that it cannot be swept away without an extensive revision of the law.
Many dominion statutes and also many provincial statutes make reference to "British subjects." It is necessary for the operation of these statutes that this term be defined in our Canadian law. If the term "British subject"
were to be dropped from the bill the result would be great confusion and uncertainty as to the application of many existing statutes. In questions of interpretation, if the meaning of the term "British subject" were not set forth as is now done in the bill, the courts would probably find it necessary to refer to the definition of "British subject" as it was recognized by the law prior to the enactment of a statutory definition. Under the common law there was no naturalization and, in general, only persons born to the status were British subjects. This would mean that, practically speaking, only persons boro in His Majesty's territories and allegiance would be British subjects. A person naturalized as a Canadian citizen would probably not be a British subject. In the same way, if we change the bill to say that "a Canadian citizen is a subject of His Majesty," rather than have the present section which says that "a Canadian citizen is a British subject," there again arises in cases of the interpretation of the statutes the question "whether this is the equivalent of making Canadian citizens British subjects for the purposes of our law.
The application of statutes in which reference is made to British subjects would be exceedingly difficult. Either the term "subject *of His Majesty" would be construed to mean a British subject, in which case we might as well use that term and be done with it, or it would not be so construed1, in which case the application of a large number of statutes would be materially altered, with a result which we cannot prophesy.
What it amounts to is this: If we do not provide for Canadian citizenship also having the status of British subjects, it will necessitate the reexamination of a large number of statutes by us, and more particularly by provincial governments. I include in that not only the provinces of Quebec and Ontario but every one of our nine provinces. There would certainly have to be extensive amendments made to many acts. So much for section 26.
Section 28 can be dealt with very briefly. It will be noted that what it does is to say that certain non-Canadians are to have the status of British subjects in Canada. The reasons for including this section are of the same order as those far including section 26. The broad argument as a symbol of association is the same, and the practical legal consideration is almost identical. If section 28 were not included there would again be the danger of confusion as to the meaning of our present statute law. Until the law is changed there would be considerable difficulty and confusion.

So far as the consequences of section 28 are concerned, in terms of rights, duties and privileges for non-Canadian British subjects, these obviously depend upon the terms and provisions of Canadian law. If we use the term "British subject" often in our statutes, section 28 may mean a great deal. If we use the term rarely, the section may mean relatively little. It all depends upon the state of our law.
The house has given this measure its wide approval and endorsation, largely because we are determined, all of us, regardless of our political convictions, to create as the paramount status of our country that of Canadian citizenship, enjoying at the same time the common status of British subject; for we must not forget that we are a free nation within the Commonwealth. We must no fail to recognize the danger of the implications which are involved in the two extremes to which I referred in the course of my remarks to-night.
This bill has won not only the approval of this house in principle, but because I promised the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) that I would do so to-night, I may say that it has won the approval of the government of Australia. The Ottawa Journal of April 9 contained a report that Prime Minister Chifley had announced that the Australian government had approved the principles embodied in the Canadian citizenship bill and proposed to set up an act along the same lines. That represents on the part of Australia, no less than on our part, a simple desire to create within that country, as in this country, a feeling that all the people belong to the country. In the case of Canada they belong to a country which in the light of its history and achievements has the right to be able to give to its citizens the designation which the people in every other country of the world save ourselves thus far, except for the limited purposes of the Immigration Act, have enjoyed.
During the debate the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) in an extremely able speech suggested that we should try to avoid hyphens, that we should try to avoid differences of race and religion. I can only say that this bill seeks to do that very thing. It will not do for hon. gentlemen to suggest that one group is less loyal to the commonwealth than another group, as has been suggested during the debate this afternoon. I take second place to no one in this house in my loyalty to the king and to the institutions of the British commonwealth, and I am sure that that is true of every hon. member in this house. Instead of trying for one purpose or another to create divisions in this country, instead of trying to create strawmen only to

knock them down, if we would seek to emphasize the common benefits of being members of the Canadian family we would be subscribing to the creating of a healthier condition in this country.
What we are trying to do basically by this bill, in the light of the development of Canada to-day as a nation, is to give to her citizens the right to be able to use a common designation which will apply to all whether they live on the Pacific or the Atlantic coast, whether they are French, English, Irish or Scandinavian or what you will, to give them a right to be able to say proudly, "We are citizens of Canada, we owe loyalty to a common king." I submit with great respect that by no stretch of the imagination can that be construed as a violation of the freedom which we enjoy as a people.
I referred to the desirability, instead of trying to pit one group against another, instead of trying to measure loyalty to Canada or to the crown, of considering an example which I think is a notable one in this country. I refer to what has been done by the university of western Ontario, a non-denominational university in my part of the country. I am sure the hon. member for London (Mr. Man-ross) will subscribe wholeheartedly to what I am going to say because he is as familiar with this work as I am. A number of years ago Doctor Sherwood Fox, a Canadian of Anglo-Saxon origin, whose love for Canada, by his own record, I think is as great as that of any man in this country, sought to give to the students of that university an understanding of Quebec by creating a summer school at Trois Pistoles, which I believe is in the riding of my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Temiscouata.

That was done to instruct English-speaking Canadians in the culture and language of French Canada. That is the kind of thing we should be doing instead of constantly measuring our loyalty, the loyalty of one group as compared with another; instead of saying, "I am more loyal than you are; my whole record shows it." I believe that the example of Doctor Fox in western Ontario is an example that all of us in this house without exception might well seek to emulate. I understand that at the present time a group in the province of Quebec are seeking to establish a school in Ontario to which their students can go and have the same opportunities of subscribing to desirable outside influences. Those are the things which we as members of this house should seek to empha-

size instead of for one purpose or another trying to use devices that can only divide, that cannot bring us more closely together.
I join with what has been said by other hon. gentlemen in paying a tribute, not only to those who have come into our Canadian family as British subjects but to those who have come from other parts of the world, some of whom are in this house. I could not avoid feeling impressed when I heard the speech of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), a man whom I have known for a long time. He comes from my own city. He was born in Russia; he came to Canada as a young lad and sold papers on the streets. His mother and father undertook the most menial tasks in the city of Windsor in order to give their children an opportunity to get along. That man is now a member of this House of Commons and was a former member of the government of Ontario. We should be proud of such people and their achievements. We should be proud of these people who are seeking to enter our Canadian family, whether they come from Yugoslavia or any other country. If we look upon them as being entitled to citizenship, then we should accord them all the privileges without creating unnecessarily divisions as between them and other potential Canadian citizens. It is only with that spirit that we shall build the kind of national fibre that everyone in this house really wants.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) said to-day that this bill by itself will not make true citizens. He went on to praise the bill and commended it to the house. I agree with him that it will not make citizens, but it will remove some of the confusion and anomalies that exist in the Canadian Nationals Act, and in the Immigration Act, and inadequacies in the Naturalization Act. It will give legal emphasis to something which in our schools, in our homes and in our churches, throughout the whole of our national life, we can do if we really want to.
A week ago in a Canadian newspaper I came across the following; and while I am not given to quoting poetry I wish to quote this to the house to-night because of the lesson given in its words, and particularly having in mind' their author. This poem was written by Percy J. Philip, a member of the Press Gallery who was president of the gallery last year. He has put into words something that I know will kindle the hearts of every member of this house. He has written:
To Canada our fathers came And gave this unknown land its name This Canada of ours;
God grant that we will never let That name be tarnished or forget The joy of building mightier yet This Canada of ours.
Out of the rivalry and strife Of older peoples came to life This Canada of ours;
They fought for what they thought was good;
God. in His mercy, understood And formed into a brotherhood This Canada of ours.
In strength together we -will stand, Defending our beloved land,
This Canada of ours;
And never shall it cease to be,
A nation where all men are free In unity from sea to sea This Canada of ours.
Those words, put into writing by a distinguished journalist, now a resident in this country, a former resident of the United Kingdom who for twenty years served a great newspaper in France, subscribe to what I know we in this house and our children and our children's children will come to regard as the standard by which real Canadianism will be judged.
My final words in moving the second reading of this bill are these. Fortune has placed this country in the position where its people do not all speak the same language and do not all adore God at the same altar. Our task is to mould all these elements into one community without destroying the richness of any of those cultural sources from which ma-^ our people have sprung. No one, I think, has gripped the need of meeting this problem of the Canadian mosaic better than a great former prime minister of this country, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who said, speaking to a group of students at the university of Toronto of the necessity of trying to have groups in Canada understand one another; "Three years ago I visited in England one of those models of gothic architecture which the hands of genius guided by an unerring faith had moulded into a harmonious whole. This cathedral was made of oak, of granite and of marble. It is the image of the nation I want to see Canada become. I want the marble to remain the marble; I want the oak to remain the oak; I want the granite to remain the granite; and out of these elements I would build a nation great among the nations of the world."

I wish to ask the minister a couple of questions. When we are conferring British citizenship on Canadian citizens, we do confer the same privilege upon all citizens of the British empire, so far as the empire as a whole is concerned, in relation to Canadian citizenship. As regards the five years' residence, the minister said that it was the same as it was in 1910. But times have changed since then and people are going from one part of the empire to another. This is taking place in all parts of the British empire, and I do not see why a man in one part of the empire should be treated the same as people outside the empire.
The main reason I rose was to make this statement. One would have thought there were only one or two classes of people in Canada who really desire to have Canadian citizenship; but as a matter of fact, for quite a long time, we have had "new Canadians" as well as old Canadians. We have had' Italians, loyal Germans, Ukrainians. Polish people, Russians. All these people came to this country a lopg while ago and they wish to have Canadian citizenship. They wish to be Canadians. For that reason I am anxious to see this bill passed. I am supporting the bill. What I wish to see, however, is that citizenship does not become a mere formality, that people will simply go and obtain citizenship without any trouble at all. There should be a decent ceremony in connection with the granting of citizenship, and people should be taught to be really good Canadian citizens. I wish to see prospective citizens made aware of the obligations which will devolve upon them in relation to the privileges which they will enjoy as a result of being Canadian citizens. I want to see them properly instructed so that they may get a reasonable idea of the history of this country and of the great traditions of their forefathers. There are great traditions so far as the great French race in Canada is concerned ; there are great traditions so far as the great English race in Canada is concerned; there are great traditions so far as the German races, the Ukrainian races and others are concerned; and all that history, all that sort of thing, the good being carefully sifted from the bad, should be taught prospective citizens. They should be told what mistakes have been

made in history. Inly in that way shall we get something worth while out of our Canadian citizenship.
I do not agree with the idea of simply making people Canadian citizens without proper instruction. That will result in nothing worth while. We must have a unified educational system in Canada, a system which will teach people to be good Canadian citizens and which will teach them the best that we have in Canada.
We have to get rid of all the old festering sores that we have had, between the races in this country. We must get rid of all the bad things and teach people that the brotherhood of man in Canada will mean something to them and that being a Canadian citizen will be worth while.
I am certainly in favour of this bill, but I think that any British subject in the commonwealth of nations, with laws similar to our own, should be allowed to become a Canadian citizen without any fuss or feathers so long as he has become a British citizen in some other part of the commonwealth. I have nothing more to say except this. We must teach the traditions pertaining to all the good which we have acquiredi in the past, or this bill will not prove of any value.

Then there was the Canadian Nationals Act introduced into this house by the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Doherty. It is true that thlt act did seek to define for a specific purpose what we call a Canadian national.

My hon. friend says that it was creating a Canadian nationality, but with great respect I say that it was not. What the act in its specific terms did was to give a definition of "Canadian citizenship" by reference. By reference to what? By reference to the Immigration Act, about which I shall have something to say in a moment.
We had become signatories to the peace treaties; we were members of the league of nations; we had adhered to the statute of the permanent court of international justice. Because there was no such designation in the the Immigration Act of a national the government of the day felt that in order to overcome what seemed to be a legal difficulty there should be an act called the Canadian Nationals Act which had as its purpose the enabling of Canadians to hold certain designated offices under some of the organizations set up by the treaties of peace. That was the purpose of that act. Speaking in the house, the then Minister of Justice indicated that it was intended to be nothing else. He was faced with the sort of questions that we have been faced with in this debate, that by trying to create a Canadian nationality we were breaking up the commonwealth and so on. In order that he would not be faced with that difficulty in the light of public opinion in this country twenty-seven years ago he brought in that act for those limited purposes. The important thing about the Canadian Nationals Act is that it really had no definition at all except for one minor purpose. Its definition of "citizenship" was a definition by reference to section 2 of the Immigration Act.
The anomalous position created as a result of the act of 1919 was that the only designation of citizenship in this country was to be found in the Immigration Act. No country in the world has ever defined its citizens by a similar measure. The result is that until this bill becomes law the only class of people

who receive the legal designation of citizen are those people who come into Canada from the outside. In other words, the hon. member for Temiscouata, myself, and other hon. members in this house; my genial friend, the hon. member for Calgary West, for whom I have great affection, and many others in Canada are not now entitled to the legal designation of Canadian citizen. This bill will go one step farther than the provisions of the Immigration Act and the restricted meaning of the Canadian Nationals Act. As a result, all who are in fact citizens of Canada will achieve this status by law.
Another thing this bill will do is to remove another anomaly that can exist under the Canadian Nationals Act and the Immigration Act. A person who has never lived in Canada, who may live in Europe, who is the son or daughter of a Canadian national may under the provisions of the Canadian Nationals Act be granted a passport and yet under the provisions of the Immigration Act be denied entry into Canada. Imagine such a thing as a Canadian national being denied entry to his own country! That was the anomalous situation which created all kinds of confusion and it is one of the things which will be a matter of history when this bill becomes law.
